notes: Stake as a cordon and pinch out side shoots. Plant out after mid-May; the most reliable tomato outdoors.
Ribbed French beefsteak, semi-determinate and early. Stake firmly; limit to 4–5 trusses outdoors.
Classic Italian plum tomato for sauce and passata. Indeterminate: stake and remove side shoots.
Pale yellow, medium-hot pods ripening red; pickle or stuff. Plant out after mid-May into warm soil.
Hungarian spice paprika (fűszerpaprika) as grown at Szeged and Kalocsa; dry red pods on strings.
Long bull's-horn sweet pepper ripening red or yellow; sweetest fully coloured. Stake when fruiting.
Thin, hot red pods that dry well for flakes and powder. Thrives in large pots on a sunny balcony.
Needs the warmest, most sheltered spot or a greenhouse; limit to 4–6 fruits per plant outdoors.
Train up strings or netting; sow outdoors late May. Water evenly and pick young to keep it cropping.
Small cornichon type; pick every 2–3 days for pickling with dill. Sprawls or climbs a low trellis.
Dark green, very productive bush courgette. Harvest at 15–20 cm; two plants feed a family.
Glossy golden-yellow fruits on an open bush. Pick small and often; easy to spot among the leaves.
Long trailing vines; plant on rich soil or the edge of the compost heap. Cure fruit in sun before storing.
Sold as Hokkaido in Central Europe: small orange fruits with edible skin. Stores until midwinter.
Needs a long warm season; choose early cultivars in Central Europe. Stores for 3–6 months.
Hull-less seeds for pumpkin-seed oil and roasting; a staple of Austrian Styria and Slovenia.
Small orange-fleshed French cantaloupe; needs heat: black mulch, cloche or greenhouse in cool areas.
Needs a long, hot summer; where summers are cool, grow small icebox types on black mulch.
Scarlet flowers, then long pods; grow up 2.5 m canes or a fence. Known as Feuerbohne in Germany.
Sow from mid-May every 3 weeks until July; needs no support. Traditionally paired with summer savory.
Old French filet bean; pick pencil-thin pods every 2 days for the finest haricots verts.
Classic German pole bean with long stringless pods. Grow 4–6 plants around each 2.5 m pole.
Sow Feb–Apr as soon as the soil is workable; pinch out the tips once pods set to deter blackfly.
Sow from March in double rows along twiggy sticks or netting. Pick often to keep pods coming.
Plant in blocks, not single rows, for wind pollination. Ripe about 3 weeks after the silks turn brown.
Plant chitted tubers in April and earth up as shoots grow. Earlies lifted in June, maincrop Aug–Sept.
Plant sets Mar–Apr 10 cm apart. Stop watering once the leaves topple; dry bulbs in the sun.
Each bulb splits into a cluster of 6–12. Plant in early spring with the tips just showing.
Plant cloves Oct–Nov for the biggest bulbs; lift in July when the lower leaves turn yellow.
Drop pencil-thick seedlings into deep dibber holes in June. Hardy; harvest from autumn through winter.
Sow thinly Mar–Jul in light, stone-free soil; fine mesh or rows of onions deter carrot fly.
Sow fresh seed Mar–Apr; slow to germinate. Roots sweeten after frost and can be lifted all winter.
Sow Apr–Jul; each 'seed' is a cluster, so thin to 10 cm. The young leaves are eaten like chard.
Long season: sow indoors in March, plant out shallowly in May. Keep moist and strip side roots.
Central European soup root (Wurzelpetersilie, petrezselyemgyökér, pietruszka). Sow Mar–Apr.
Ready in 4–6 weeks: sow small batches every 2 weeks Mar–May and again in Sept. Keep moist.
Large white Bavarian 'Radi', sliced and salted for the beer garden. Sow Apr–Jul; thin to 15 cm.
Central European favourite; harvest at tennis-ball size. Even watering prevents woody, split bulbs.
Violet-blue bulbs with white flesh; early and quick. Sow under glass in February for May harvests.
Crinkled, very hardy winter cabbage (Wirsing, kel); harvest Oct–Feb. Plant firmly in rich soil.
Firm heads for sauerkraut and winter storage. Needs rich soil; net against cabbage white caterpillars.

latin: Brassica oleracea var. capitata f. rubra
notes: Purple-red heads for braising (Rotkohl, Blaukraut). Slow growing: plant out by June. Stores well.
Needs rich soil and steady moisture. Fold leaves over the curd to keep it white as it matures.
Cut the main head while buds are tight; side shoots follow for weeks. Sow Apr–Jun.
Long-season winter crop picked from the base upwards Oct–Feb. Firm soil and stake on windy sites.
Cool-season crop: sow Mar–Apr and Aug–Sept, as it bolts in summer heat. Winter types overwinter.
Cut-and-come-again leaves from June until hard frost; copes with heat better than spinach.
Stems in red, pink, orange, yellow and white; ornamental enough for flower borders and pots.
Compact, sweet semi-cos; sow little and often from March. Ideal for tight spaces and containers.
Loose red oak-leaf type; pick outer leaves for weeks. Slow to bolt and pretty as an edging.
Frilly, red-edged Italian loose-leaf lettuce; colours best in full sun. Pick leaves or whole heads.
Sow Aug–Sept for winter salads (Feldsalat, Nüsslisalat); fully hardy. Sow on a firm seedbed.
Peppery leaves in 4–6 weeks. Sow in spring and late summer; bolts and attracts flea beetle in heat.
Sow Jun–Jul for autumn salads; cover the centre with a plate for a week to blanch the heart.
Sow Jun–Jul; heads turn deep red as nights get cold. Hardy enough for late-autumn harvests.
Lemony perennial leaves for soups and sauces (oseille, sóska). Cut off flower stems to keep leaves coming.
Cut buds before the scales open; leave a few to flower for bees. Mulch the crowns over winter.
Grown for blanched leaf stalks: tie up and wrap plants 3–4 weeks before the autumn harvest.
Plant crowns in light, sandy soil; cut spears from year 3, April until 24 June. Beds last 15–20 years.
Pull stalks Apr–June only, none in the first year. Remove flower spikes; mulch with manure in winter.
Kren (AT), torma (HU), chrzan (PL). Regrows from any root fragment, so grow it in a sunk bucket.
Topinambur: knobbly tubers dug Nov–Mar. Invasive, as every missed tuber regrows; use a root barrier.
Sow after mid-June to avoid bolting; keep evenly moist and earth up the swelling bulbs.
Schwarzwurzel or 'winter asparagus': sow Mar–Apr in deep, loose soil; lift the roots Oct–Mar.
Evergreen subshrub; trim lightly after flowering and replace every 4–5 years when it gets woody.
Dusky purple-grey leaves with the same flavour; a fine foil for pink and silver plants. Needs drainage.
Native butterfly magnet (Dost). Cut back after flowering; flavour is strongest on poor, dry soil.
Tender; grown as an annual (Majoran, majoránna). Sow indoors in April. Key for potato soup and sausages.
Evergreen dwarf subshrub with peppery leaves for beans. Makes a good low edging for herb beds.
Bohnenkraut, the classic annual herb for green beans; sow from May between the bean rows.
Sterile: buy plants, not seed (seed gives coarse Russian tarragon). Needs sharp winter drainage.
Delicate anise flavour (cerfeuil, Kerbel). Sow spring and late summer in light shade; bolts in heat.
Biennial grown yearly; sow Mar–Jul, germination takes 3–4 weeks. A neat edging for potager beds.
Stronger flavour than curly parsley; cut outer stems first. Avoid sowing where parsley grew last year.
Essential for Central European pickles, soups and sauces. Sow in situ every 3 weeks; self-seeds.
Bolts fast in heat: sow every 3 weeks Apr–Aug for leaves, or let it flower for the seed.
Maggikraut: one plant is plenty for soups and stocks. A long-lived Bauerngarten perennial.
Lemon-scented tea herb (Zitronenmelisse, citromfű). Cut back after flowering to stop self-seeding.
Classic tea mint (Pfefferminze). Very invasive: plant in a sunk pot and divide every 3 years.
Semi-evergreen and loved by bees and butterflies. Clip in spring; makes a low hedge for knot gardens.
Edible blue star flowers and a top bee plant. Annual that self-seeds freely around the veg garden.
Annual tea herb (Kamille, kamilla); surface-sow in spring or autumn. Pick flowers when fully open.
Apple-scented evergreen mat; the non-flowering 'Treneague' is used for chamomile lawns and seats.
Intensely lemony tea leaves (verveine). Tender: overwinter pots frost-free; leafs out late in spring.
Biennial: leafy rosette in year 1, flowers and seed (Kümmel, kömény) in year 2. Native meadow plant.
Perennial fennel for leaves and seed; swallowtail food plant. Keep away from dill to avoid crossing.
Vigorous and very upright, one of the hardier rosemaries. Works as a low informal hedge in warm spots.
Trails over walls and pot rims; less hardy than upright forms and needs perfect drainage.
Lemon-scented leaves for fish, chicken and teas. Trim after flowering to keep it compact.
Native mat-former (Quendel) for paving cracks, rock gardens and dry banks; a magnet for bees.
Ready to cut in 1–2 weeks; sow on the windowsill year-round or outdoors every 10 days.
Cucumber-flavoured leaves (pimprenelle); one of the seven herbs of Frankfurt green sauce.
Spine-free summer canes; tie to wires and cut fruited canes to the ground straight after picking.
Fruits on the current year's canes from August; cut all canes to the ground in late winter.
Thornless, semi-erect canes; fan-train on wires, plants 2–3 m apart. Heavy crops from August.
Ripens around St John's Day (Johannisbeere). Prune to an open goblet; also trains as fence cordons.
Translucent, sweet white berries; an old French cultivar (Blanche de Versailles). Prune as redcurrant.
Fruits on young wood: each winter remove a third of the oldest stems at the base. Aromatic leaves.
Thorny; pick some green in June for cooking, the rest ripe in July. Choose mildew-resistant cultivars.
Thornless blackcurrant × gooseberry cross; vigorous and resistant to mildew and big-bud mite.
Needs acid soil (pH 4–5.5) or ericaceous compost; water with rainwater. Plant two cultivars.
Earliest berry, ripe late May (jagoda kamczacka); extremely hardy. Needs two cultivars to set fruit.
Tiny aromatic fruits June–Oct (fraises des bois). Runnerless types make a neat edging for paths.
Blackberry × raspberry hybrid with large, aromatic dark-red fruit. Train on wires like blackberries.
Tart, vitamin-rich berries for juice and jam, popular in Poland and Czechia. White May flowers, red autumn.
Ringelblume, körömvirág: edible petals; self-seeds. Deadhead and it flowers until frost.
Peppery edible leaves and flowers; flowers best in poor soil. Climbing types scramble to 2 m.
Sow in pots Feb–Mar or direct in April; grow up 2 m netting. Pick daily to keep it flowering.
Sow direct in autumn or March on poor soil; a cornfield annual that self-seeds. Petals are edible.
Scatter seed on disturbed soil in autumn or early spring; resents transplanting. Self-seeds.
Seed poppy (Mohn, mák) with grey leaves and fine seed heads. Germany requires a permit to grow it.
Jungfer im Grünen: sow direct Mar–Apr or Sept; the inflated seed pods dry well. Self-seeds.
Pinch young plants for bushiness; tall types make long-lasting cut flowers. A bumblebee favourite.
Sow under glass in April or direct in late May; hates cold. A cut-and-come-again flower for vases.
Pure white single flowers above feathery foliage; more flowers in lean soil. Deadhead regularly.
Orange and yellow cosmos for hot, dry spots; compact types suit edging and pots.
Dwarf sunflower with fluffy, fully double golden blooms; good in pots and children's gardens.
Branching, with many cream flowers and dark centres over a long season. Birds take the seed.
Tall, drooping white trumpets scented at dusk above big leaf rosettes. Sow indoors in March.
White flowers open and release scent in the evening; plant near seating. Tolerates light shade.
Airy pink, white or purple heads on tall, spiny stems; musky scent. Sow under glass in March.
Long crimson tassels for late-summer drama and drying. Sow under glass in April, plant out late May.
Lacy white umbels for cutting; autumn sowings flower earlier. Sap can irritate skin in sunlight.
Flat lacy umbels with showy outer petals. Sow in autumn or March; self-seeds lightly.
Pincushion heads from near-black to pink; a butterfly favourite with a long cutting season.
Annual delphinium: sow direct in autumn or March, as it dislikes transplanting. All parts toxic.
Silky orange cups that close in dull weather; thrives in poor, dry soil. Sow direct; self-seeds.
Bienenweide: top bee plant and green manure, flowering 6–8 weeks after sowing. Dig in before seeding.
Large pompon heads in orange and yellow; a Central European bedding classic. Deadhead often.
Clouds of small single flowers over citrus-scented leaves; petals are edible in salads.
Classic bold red bedding and balcony plant. Plant out after mid-May and feed regularly.
Slender violet-blue spikes all summer, much visited by bees. Tender perennial grown as an annual.
The window-box classic (Geranie, muskátli). Tender perennial: overwinter cool and bright at 5–10 °C.
Trailing geranium of Alpine balconies, cascading 60–100 cm. Feed weekly through the summer.
Rose-scented leaves for teas, jellies and cakes; most plants sold are P. 'Graveolens' hybrids.
Bedding and balcony staple; feed weekly and deadhead. Small-flowered multiflora types cope best with rain.
Vigorous trailing petunias cascading up to 1 m from balcony boxes; grown from cuttings. Feed weekly.
Neat, nonstop edging for sun or shade; bronze-leaved types take full sun best.
Fleißiges Lieschen: bright colour for shade. Prone to downy mildew; keep evenly moist.
Larger flowers and bronze leaves; takes more sun than busy Lizzie and resists downy mildew.
Mats of blue for bed edges, boxes and baskets. Trim after the first flush and never let it dry out.
Sold as Verbena × hybrida: trailing flower clusters for baskets and boxes; visited by butterflies.
Fluffy lavender-blue edging (Leberbalsam), a compact bedding classic. Deadhead to keep it flowering.
Honey-scented white carpets for edging and paving; draws hoverflies whose larvae eat aphids.
Feathery plumes in red, orange and yellow that dry well. Needs warmth: plant out in late May.
Clover-like magenta, pink or white heads; an everlasting for drying. Loves heat and sun.
Sow under glass Feb–Mar for golden daisies July to frost. Short-lived perennial; often self-seeds.
Syn. Lavatera trimestris: satiny pink or white trumpets all summer. Sow direct in April.
Levkoje: clove-scented spikes for cutting and cottage beds. Sow under glass in March.
Golden stars on trailing stems for balcony boxes; tough in heat and wind, and loved by bees.
Tender shrub used as balcony bedding (listed as annual). Overwinter cool and frost-free; cut back.
